item.title: Interwar
item.description: I do like a handsome building; I think everyone does. Architecture directly affects our daily experience of life like no other art. I expect most people have strong opinions about what they like in a building and what they dislike. I certainly do. Yet, despite having those strong opinions, I’ve very rarely read a book about architecture, and if you asked me to count off some famous architects I doubt I’d exhaust the fingers of one hand. With my elderly Mum in a nursing home in Hastings, I’ve found myself regularly stopping off for lunch on my fortnightly visits at the De La Warr Pavilion in Bexhill. It’s proclaimed as a modernist masterpiece; it certainly is a very impressive building; the circular staircase alone is worth making a trip to see. It was built in the 1930s and must have appeared as a spaceship on the promenade of the otherwise quite dowdy Bexhill. One of the delights of a visit there is the excellent bookshop, with its collection of works on architecture and design. It was while browsing the shelves that I first came across this book. I must have picked it up half a dozen times before deciding to buy a copy. I decided that I needed an education in architecture, and what better way to start than to fit this into my interwar reading list. It was published posthumously; the author, Gavin Stamp, had died in 2017 leaving the unfinished manuscript. His wife organised its publication and it was finally released in 2024. Stamp was a prolific journalist and architectural historian, and a founder and the first chairman of the Thirties Society, now the Twentieth Century Society, which aims to preserve notable buildings of the period. He was apparently one of the leading campaigners who saved both Battersea and Bankside power stations; the latter is now the Tate Modern.

item.title: The Long Weekend
item.description: I can’t remember where I heard about this book. It was on my long Amazon wish list for a while, until one Christmas a few years back when Leo, my son, chose it as my present. Since then it’s sat in my bookshelf waiting patiently to be read until it found its way onto my 2026 interwar reading list. It’s a survey of aristocratic British country house life between the wars, so an obvious choice. By the time I got around to reading it, Leo had long forgotten giving it to me and was surprised when I told him he was the original purchaser. I don’t know much about Adrian Tinniswood the author. Wikipedia tells me he is professor of history at the University of Buckingham and a trustee of the National Trust. He is a prolific author and has written books on Christopher Wren, The Royal Society, and architecture, but he specialises in the British aristocracy and their houses. This is the second book I’ve read this year titled “The Long Weekend”. He freely admits that he borrowed the title from the Robert Graves book. It’s a large format paperback with lots of pictures, published in 2016.
